headline: Peanut Bunker Balling Up on Stratford Shoal — Blues Are All Over It, Bass Still Waiting Their Turn
subhead: The bait tells the story this week: bunker schools tightening under bird activity from the Norwalk Islands to Middle Ground, and it's the bluefish cashing in first.
body_markdown:
Watch the bait before you watch the boats and this week made its case again. Peanut bunker started balling tight off Stratford Shoal and around Middle Ground Light in the last ten days, pushed into nervous, flickering pods by everything underneath them. Gulls and terns have been working the surface in short, violent bursts — the kind of bird play that tells you blues are underneath punching through, not just picking. Get closer and you can see the bunker doing what bunker do when they're scared: balling tight, dimpling the surface, then scattering in a spray when something big comes through from below. That's been the read across the Central Sound rip line all week, from the Norwalk Islands stretching east across to the Connecticut shore and down toward Charles Island.

The water is still carrying summer heat. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and even out toward New London it's holding near 69 — that's a shallow, forgiving gradient that's kept bait comfortable and slow to push out, which is exactly why the bunker schools have had time to build density instead of scattering east early like some years. Warmer water on the western and central end of the Sound versus the cooler eastern stretch has essentially parked the biomass right in our zone, and the bluefish have noticed first.

That lines up with what the 44th Annual Surfside Hotel tournament fleet has been finding working the western Sound and pushing into Central Sound structure — bluefish have been the most consistent predator around all week, and they're not subtle about it. Boats working bunker schools off Stratford Shoal and out toward the Norwalk Islands have been getting into choppers in the 4- to 8-pound class, some bigger, on straight bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 20 to 35 feet, and on wire-leadered Ava jigs and diamond jigs worked through the middle of the bait balls on the last two hours of the ebb. When the tide's really ripping through the Stratford Shoal cut, a simple bucktail bounced off bottom and swung through the current seam has been drawing hits too — the blues are using that current the same way stripers do, sitting on the downcurrent edge and letting the tide do the work.

Stripers are a different story right now, and it's worth being straight about it — they're in a holding pattern. There are fish around Middle Ground and scattered through the Norwalk Islands, but they're not committing in blitz numbers yet, and the honest read is that the bait hasn't concentrated enough to force the issue. That should change. The moon is building toward full, which means more tidal push, which means these bunker schools currently spread loosely from the Sound's midline down toward the CT shoreline should tighten up further in the next week to ten days. When that happens, expect the stripers already staged nearby to commit hard, the way they always do once bait gets pinned against structure instead of drifting free. Until then, the better bass move has been working eel or bunker chunks on the bottom around Stratford Shoal on the tail of the ebb, or dragging a swimming plug through the rip when the tide is really moving — fish are there, but you're earning them one at a time rather than into a blitz.

Fluke have done exactly what late August fluke do, which is soften without disappearing. We said last week this looked like a normal seasonal slide rather than a collapse, and that's held — fluke are still coming off the deeper channel edges around Port Jefferson Harbor mouth and the drop-offs near the Norwalk Islands, mostly on white and chartreuse Gulp paired with a light bucktail, worked slow on the last of the outgoing when the current lays down enough to keep bottom contact. Sizes have been mixed, plenty of shorts mixed with keeper-class fish in the 18 to 21-inch range, and the bite window is tightening to that slower water rather than running all tide long. Porgies remain a dependable afternoon fill-in around the rockier structure off Charles Island and the Norwalk Islands on the incoming, small hooks and sandworms doing the job, and blackfish are still a touch early — worth checking again once the water starts to actually cool rather than just holding steady.

Looking at the next few days, don't expect a dramatic shift. The bluefish should keep tracking the bunker schools hard through Labor Day week — that's been the most reliable pattern in the zone all month and there's no reason for it to break unless the bait scatters. Watch Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground closely for signs the bait is tightening further as the moon builds; that's the tell that stripers are about to switch from holding pattern to feeding mode. And keep half an eye east — bonito have been pushing west out of Rhode Island waters, and if that continues, the Race and the eastern approaches to the Sound are the first place a Central Sound angler would see it show up. Nothing on the board yet locally, but that's exactly the kind of thing you catch by watching the bait, not the forecast.
